subject: Economics
description: Bank nationalisation (1969, 1980), Narasimham Committees, Basel norms, IBC 2016

questions.stem: The first major nationalisation of commercial banks in India took place in:

options.option_text: August 1947
July 1969 — 14 large private banks were nationalised
April 1980
January 1949 — when RBI was nationalised

questions.explanation: First wave — 19 July 1969, PM Indira Gandhi nationalised 14 private banks (each with deposits ≥ ₹50 crore). Aims: priority sector lending (agriculture, small industry), branch expansion in rural areas, control over credit policy. Second wave — 15 April 1980, 6 more banks nationalised (deposits ≥ ₹200 crore). RBI itself was nationalised earlier (1 January 1949). Imperial Bank → State Bank of India in 1955 (a third nationalisation thread). New Bank of India was merged into PNB in 1993.
questions.subject: Economics

options.option_text: Nationalisation of all private banks
Reduction in CRR/SLR, prudential norms (capital adequacy, NPA classification), deregulation of interest rates
Banning of private banks
Repeal of the Banking Regulation Act

questions.explanation: M. Narasimham Committee on Financial System (1991) — landmark reforms in liberalisation era: reduce CRR (was 15%) and SLR (was 38%) progressively; introduce capital adequacy ratio (Basel I) of 8%; recognise non-performing assets (NPAs); open up to new private banks (HDFC, ICICI, UTI, Axis, IndusInd, Yes — all post-1994 entrants). Narasimham II (1998) — focused on consolidation, computerisation, autonomy for boards. Both committees triggered most modern banking reforms.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: An asset is classified as a 'Non-Performing Asset' (NPA) by RBI if interest / principal remains overdue for:

options.option_text: 30 days
90 days
180 days
1 year

questions.explanation: NPA — overdue beyond 90 days (one quarter). Sub-classifications: Standard (paying), Sub-standard (NPA up to 12 months), Doubtful (NPA 12-36 months), Loss (over 36 months — written off / negligible recovery expected). Banks must make 'provisions' (set aside profits) for NPAs — Standard 0.4%, Sub-standard 15%, Doubtful 25-100%, Loss 100%. Twin-balance-sheet problem (2014-18) was driven by surge in corporate NPAs. Net NPA ratio of scheduled commercial banks dropped to ~0.7% by 2024 (peak ~12% in 2018).
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, India was passed in:
questions.explanation: IBC, 2016 — passed Lok Sabha 5 May 2016, RS 11 May 2016, President's assent 28 May 2016. Provides 180-day timeline (extendable +90 days; later capped at 330 days) for resolving stressed corporate debtors. Replaced fragmented insolvency laws (SICA, RDDBFI Act, etc.). Apex authority — IBBI (Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India). Major resolutions — Essar Steel (sold to ArcelorMittal Nippon Steel, 2019), Bhushan Steel (sold to Tata Steel), Jet Airways. Has improved NPA recovery rates significantly.

questions.stem: The 'Basel III' norms — international banking regulation framework — focus primarily on:

options.option_text: Country credit ratings
Bank capital adequacy, leverage ratio, liquidity standards (LCR, NSFR)
Currency exchange rates only
Income tax for banks

questions.explanation: Basel III — agreed by Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS, 27 jurisdictions) post-2008 financial crisis. Key requirements: minimum CET-1 capital 4.5%, Tier 1 capital 6%, total capital 8% of RWA + Capital Conservation Buffer 2.5% + Counter-cyclical buffer 0-2.5%. Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) ≥ 100% (30-day stress). Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR) ≥ 100% (1-year horizon). Leverage Ratio ≥ 3%. India implemented Basel III through RBI guidelines, fully phased in by 2019.

questions.stem: The first 'Payments Bank' to start operations in India (April 2017) was:

options.option_text: India Post Payments Bank
Airtel Payments Bank
Paytm Payments Bank
Fino Payments Bank

questions.explanation: Airtel Payments Bank — first to launch (January 2017 pilot, full launch April 2017). RBI granted in-principle licences to 11 entities in 2015 — 6 went live (Airtel, India Post, Paytm, Fino, Jio, NSDL). Payments banks can accept deposits (up to ₹2 lakh per customer; raised from ₹1 lakh in 2021), issue debit cards, internet banking — but CANNOT lend or issue credit cards. They must invest 75% of deposits in government securities. Dr. Nachiket Mor Committee (2014) recommended this differentiated banking licence.

questions.stem: The Bank Mergers of 1 April 2020 reduced the number of public-sector banks from 27 (in 2017) to:
questions.explanation: Public-sector bank consolidation — announced August 2019, effective 1 April 2020. Brought down PSBs to 12. Mergers: PNB + OBC + United Bank → PNB; Canara + Syndicate → Canara; Union + Andhra + Corporation → Union; Indian + Allahabad → Indian. Earlier: SBI + 5 associates + Bharatiya Mahila Bank (April 2017); Bank of Baroda + Vijaya + Dena (April 2019). Idea: fewer-but-stronger PSBs with better capital + technology + governance — 'Banking 4.0'. Current PSBs: SBI, PNB, BoB, Canara, Union, Indian, BoI, Central, IOB, UCO, BoM, P&S Bank.

questions.stem: The Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation (DICGC) insures each depositor per bank up to a maximum limit. After the enhancement announced in Union Budget 2020–21, this insured amount stands at?

options.option_text: ₹1 lakh per depositor, covering all deposit types since inception
₹5 lakh per depositor per bank, covering all types of deposits
₹2 lakh per depositor, applicable only to savings account holders
₹10 lakh per depositor, limited to nationalised bank customers only

questions.explanation: The DICGC deposit insurance limit was enhanced from ₹1 lakh to ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank (covering savings, fixed, recurring and current deposits in aggregate) as formalised by the DICGC (Amendment) Act 2021, first proposed in Union Budget 2020–21. Option A (₹1 lakh) was the pre-2020 limit — the single most common wrong answer students give because they recall the old figure.

questions.stem: As per RBI's Priority Sector Lending (PSL) guidelines, what percentage of their Adjusted Net Bank Credit (ANBC) are domestic Scheduled Commercial Banks required to direct to the priority sector?

options.option_text: 32% of ANBC, as revised under the 2015 PSL master direction
35% of ANBC, for banks with predominantly rural branch networks
40% of ANBC, as mandated by RBI's priority sector lending guidelines
45% of ANBC, applicable to banks with large urban-centric loan books

questions.explanation: RBI mandates that domestic SCBs lend 40% of ANBC (or credit equivalent of off-balance-sheet exposure, whichever is higher) to priority sectors including agriculture (18% sub-target), MSMEs, education, and housing. Option B (35%) is a common guess with no basis in RBI norms; 32% is entirely fabricated. Foreign banks with fewer than 20 branches operate on a separate phased roadmap.

questions.stem: Under PM MUDRA Yojana, a micro-enterprise seeking a collateral-free loan of ₹3 lakh to expand its tailoring unit would be classified under which MUDRA loan tier?

options.option_text: Shishu — for credit requirements up to ₹50,000 per enterprise
Kishor — for credit requirements of ₹50,001 to ₹5 lakh per unit
Tarun — for credit requirements of ₹5 lakh to ₹10 lakh per unit
Udyam — for credit requirements between ₹10 lakh and ₹50 lakh

questions.explanation: MUDRA loans are classified into three tiers: Shishu (up to ₹50,000), Kishor (₹50,001–₹5 lakh), and Tarun (₹5 lakh–₹10 lakh). A ₹3 lakh loan falls squarely in the Kishor range. 'Udyam' is the MSME registration portal under the Ministry of MSME — not a MUDRA loan category — and serves as a deliberate distractor for students who confuse the two government schemes.

questions.stem: Debt Recovery Tribunals (DRTs) were set up in India to give banks and financial institutions a faster alternative to civil courts for recovering dues. Under which legislation were DRTs formally constituted?

options.option_text: Recovery of Debts Due to Banks and Financial Institutions Act, 1993
SARFAESI Act, 2002 — which empowered banks to establish recovery tribunals
Banking Regulation Act, 1949 — amended in 1993 to create civil debt courts
Narasimham Committee (I) Report, directly codified as legislation in 1993

questions.explanation: DRTs were established under the Recovery of Debts Due to Banks and Financial Institutions (RDDBFI) Act, 1993, creating dedicated tribunals to adjudicate recovery disputes above ₹10 lakh. The SARFAESI Act (2002) came a decade later and allows banks to enforce security interest WITHOUT going to DRTs at all — making it the most tempting wrong answer, as candidates frequently conflate the two distinct recovery mechanisms.

questions.stem: Under the Basel III liquidity framework, the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) requires banks to hold sufficient High-Quality Liquid Assets (HQLA) to survive a net cash outflow stress scenario over how many calendar days?

options.option_text: 15 calendar days, the minimum liquidity window under the older Basel II norms
30 calendar days, the standard Basel III stressed liquidity time horizon
60 calendar days, as prescribed by RBI for Indian scheduled commercial banks
90 calendar days, aligned with the Net Stable Funding Ratio measurement window

questions.explanation: The LCR under Basel III mandates that a bank's HQLA stock must cover total net cash outflows over a 30-day stress period; RBI adopted the same 30-day standard for Indian banks. Option D is the most dangerous distractor — the Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR), Basel III's other key liquidity measure, actually covers a 1-year horizon, not 90 days; 90 days is a plausible-sounding but wholly incorrect value.

questions.stem: Under Section 13(2) of the SARFAESI Act, 2002, after a bank issues a written demand notice to a defaulting borrower for repayment of a secured debt, within how many days must the borrower discharge the full outstanding liability to prevent the bank from enforcing its security interest?

options.option_text: 30 days from the notice date, in line with consumer protection notice periods
45 days from the notice date, matching pre-SARFAESI debt recovery practice
60 days from the notice date, as explicitly stated in Section 13(2)
90 days from the notice date, the same window used for NPA classification

questions.explanation: Section 13(2) of the SARFAESI Act, 2002 explicitly grants borrowers 60 days after the bank's written demand notice to repay in full; on non-compliance the bank may take possession of, manage, or sell the secured asset without court intervention. Option A (30 days) confuses this with other statutory notice periods; Option D (90 days) is a high-frequency trap because 90 days is the NPA classification threshold — an entirely different regulatory metric.

questions.stem: The RBI revised its Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) framework effective January 2022. Which parameter was newly introduced as a trigger in the revised framework, replacing the earlier profitability-based trigger?

options.option_text: Gross NPA ratio crossing 10% of gross advances for two consecutive years
CASA ratio falling below 20% of total deposits for a full fiscal year
Tier 1 Leverage Ratio falling below the prescribed RBI minimum threshold
Credit-to-Deposit ratio exceeding 80% for three consecutive quarterly reviews

questions.explanation: The November 2021 PCA revision retained Capital (CRAR and CET1) and Asset Quality (NNPA ratio) as trigger parameters, but replaced the Profitability trigger (Return on Assets turning negative for two years) with a new Leverage trigger — the Tier 1 Leverage Ratio breaching its prescribed minimum. Options B (CASA ratio) and D (Credit-Deposit ratio) are never PCA parameters; Option A misrepresents the NNPA threshold, which is set well below 10% under the framework.
